content: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of various tools for detecting schistosomiasis, several methods were assessed, including proteinuria reagent strips, haematuria reagent strips, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), and indirect hemagglutination assay (IHA). These tools were analyzed for their sensitivity and specificity in detecting schistosome infections in human populations. The review also considered molecular techniques such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for amplifying schistosome DNA and antibody assays for detecting schistosome antigens using ELISA. The systematic review included studies that applied diagnostic methods for schistosomiasis in humans, focusing on key outcomes such as diagnostic sensitivity and specificity. The authors also evaluated study bias and challenges in applying the findings to real-world settings. Databases such as PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, LILACS, and Africa-Wide Information were searched, with the last search conducted in February 2021. In the meta-analysis, 17 diagnostic techniques for Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma haematobium infections were identified beyond the reference tests. The overall certainty of evidence was moderate. For diagnosing S. mansoni using 2, 4, or 6 Kato-Katz tests as the reference standard, the sensitivity of circulating cathodic antigen (CCA) urine cassette assay (version 1) was estimated at 64% (95% CI: 41–83%, 4 studies), 85% (95% CI: 76–92%, 9 studies), and 81% (95% CI: 54–95%, 4 studies), respectively. The specificity was 66% (95% CI: 43–84%), 62% (95% CI: 50–74%), and 63% (95% CI: 43–80%), respectively. Data on circulating anodic antigen (CAA) were limited, with one study estimating a sensitivity of 96% (95% CI: 79–100%) and specificity of 65% (95% CI: 60–70%) relative to Kato-Katz. The SmCTF-RDT (S. mansoni cercarial transformation fluid rapid diagnostic test) had a sensitivity of 87% (95% CI: 30–99%, 4 studies) and specificity of 35% (95% CI: 14–63%, 4 studies) compared to Kato-Katz. For S. haematobium diagnosis using urine microscopy as the reference standard, haematuria reagent strips demonstrated a sensitivity of 86% (95% CI: 58–98%, 5 studies) and specificity of 86% (95% CI: 73–96%). Proteinuria reagent strips had a sensitivity of 72% (95% CI: 24–96%, 3 studies) and specificity of 86% (95% CI: 48–99%). Other molecular-based methods, such as ELISA and PCR-based assays, lacked sufficient data to draw definitive conclusions. The certainty of evidence for diagnostic accuracy was moderate overall. A key limitation of the meta-analysis was the use of imperfect reference tests (Kato-Katz for S. mansoni and urine microscopy for S. haematobium), which have low sensitivity. This limitation hindered accurate estimation of diagnostic characteristics for newer tests with superior sensitivity. Additionally, many included diagnostic tests were not commercially available, and molecular methods often required advanced laboratory facilities, resources, and expertise. The review highlighted the need for rigorous evaluation of CCA, including the role of trace positives in representing true infections. The specificity of many parasitological diagnostics likely varies by setting and disease prevalence. Tools dependent on egg burden, which correlates with transmission intensity, are also affected. The study did not include analyses for S. japonicum. Recent reviews and meta-analyses have provided data on the sensitivity and specificity of CCA and other point-of-care diagnostic tests for schistosomiasis. A Cochrane meta-analysis estimated that CCA for S. mansoni diagnosis had a sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 55%, assuming CCA is more sensitive than stool microscopy. Another study compared prevalence estimates between Kato-Katz and CCA, finding that 5% prevalence by Kato-Katz corresponded to 20% prevalence by CCA, and 10% prevalence by Kato-Katz corresponded to 30% prevalence by CCA. Different versions of the CCA test were used in these studies. The review demonstrated the diagnostic specifications of tools for schistosomiasis in humans. While many point-of-care, molecular, and immunological methods show promise, no new diagnostic tool was identified as clearly superior to conventional methods. The certainty of diagnostic accuracy estimates was limited by the imperfect nature of reference tests, the small number of studies, and the lack of standardization in real-world settings. Many diagnostic tools require further development, characterization, and validation in field settings.
